periods.analysis: We opened the series in a strong position at 1,205,354 TEUs, comfortably green against the 1,120,000 target. The practical story behind that number is berth discipline: the South Harbor crane teams kept the MSC/Sealand and CMA CGM windows tight, and the I-595 gate appointment pilot reduced late-afternoon bunching on Routes 7 and 12. Refrigerated export boxes also held up well through the summer produce shoulder season, which gave us a balanced mix instead of a one-lane import surge. This is the kind of growth Harborview can support when terminal operations, customs exams, and inland drayage are managed as one system.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by extending the gate appointment pilot from the South Harbor lanes to the North Intermodal Yard before peak holiday imports arrive. Keep the weekly berth-window review with pilots, tugs, terminal operators, and Customs and Border Protection, with a specific focus on crane downtime over two hours. Use this quarter as the operating baseline for the 2025 carrier retention plan, especially for services that can add loaded export calls rather than empties only.

periods.analysis: Volume eased to 1,181,697 TEUs, down 23,657 from 2024-Q3, but it stayed solidly green and above target. That modest step-down is not alarming; it tracks the normal post-summer adjustment and two weather-related pilotage slowdowns in the outer channel. What I like is that the team protected fluidity even as holiday retail boxes arrived unevenly, using Pier 4 overflow stacks and temporary weekend chassis sweeps with Harborview Chassis Pool. The port did not chase volume at the expense of reliability, and that matters for keeping the gateway credible.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the weekend chassis sweep through January and publish a simple carrier-facing dashboard on dwell, turn times, and missed berth windows. Direct Marine Operations to pre-stage Pier 4 overflow plans when forecast vessel exchanges exceed 3,800 moves per call. Begin negotiating Q2 extra-loader options now, so the port can convert reliability into incremental TEUs when the market firms.

periods.analysis: 2025-Q1 slipped to 1,113,274 TEUs, down 68,423 from 2024-Q4, moving us into yellow just below the 1,120,000 target while still above the 1,020,000 red threshold. I am watchful here, not panicked: Lunar New Year blank sailings, a short refrigeration parts delay at Terminal 2, and two rail service interruptions on the inland connector all landed in the same quarter. The watch-item is loaded export recovery, because empties moved efficiently but several resin and citrus shippers held bookings after missed rail cutoffs. A yellow quarter is a signal to tighten the operating chain before customers decide the slippage is a pattern.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a 30-day Cargo Recovery Cell with the terminal operators, the Class I rail desk, customs exam station, and the top 15 drayage firms, chaired twice weekly by Port Operations. Prioritize refrigeration spares for Terminal 2 plugs R-214 through R-289 and require daily reporting until utilization and outage rates normalize. Offer targeted off-peak gate incentives for the resin and citrus export cohorts, but sunset them after the next quarter unless they produce measurable loaded-export lift.

periods.analysis: The recovery showed up in the numbers: 2025-Q2 reached 1,126,419 TEUs, up 13,145 from 2025-Q1, returning the measure to green. That is a narrow but important win because it proves the Q1 dip was manageable rather than structural. The Cargo Recovery Cell cleared the Terminal 2 reefer backlog, and the Thursday night export gate on Cargo Route East helped two citrus consolidators hit vessel cutoffs they missed in March. We are back over target, but only by 6,419 TEUs, so the operating discipline cannot relax.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Thursday night export gate through the next two vessel cycles and add a second off-peak block only if bookings exceed 900 export moves. Convert the Cargo Recovery Cell from emergency cadence to a standing monthly exception review, with rail cutoff failures and reefer outages as the first two metrics. Ask Commercial Development to lock in at least one additional summer extra-loader call from carriers that benefited from the improved Q2 reliability.

periods.analysis: 2025-Q3 delivered the breakout quarter we were positioning for: 1,235,553 TEUs, up 109,134 from 2025-Q2 and well into green. The gain was broad-based, with extra-loader calls on the Gulf-Atlantic service, stronger apparel imports, and more loaded exports from the West Harbor resin cluster. Operationally, the extended appointment windows and the new OCR lanes at Gate 6 kept truck turn times from becoming the tax on growth. This quarter tells carriers that Harborview can absorb surge volume without turning the port into a parking lot.
periods.recommendations: Sustain this momentum by making the Gate 6 OCR staffing pattern permanent for peak days and completing a cost-benefit review for adding OCR at Gate 3. Reserve two flexible berth windows in the September-October plan for extra-loader opportunities, but require carriers to provide 10-day stowage forecasts. Direct the port marketing team to use the Q3 performance package in renewal talks with the Gulf-Atlantic and Caribbean feeder services.

periods.analysis: Volume settled to 1,205,970 TEUs, down 29,583 from 2025-Q3, while remaining comfortably green and nearly matching the strong level we saw a year earlier. That decline is acceptable after the Q3 surge and reflects a cleaner, less congested peak season rather than a loss of market position. The Pier 4 overflow yard was used more selectively, and yard density stayed within the operating band at South Harbor even during the November retail push. The important point is that Harborview held the higher plateau after recovery, rather than falling back to the yellow edge.
periods.recommendations: Continue selective use of Pier 4 overflow, but set a trigger based on yard density and forecast exchanges rather than opening it by default. Renew the chassis sweep agreement with Harborview Chassis Pool for Q1 storm and holiday resilience, including a minimum pool availability clause. Begin the winter maintenance plan for cranes C-12 through C-15 now, so preventive work does not collide with the next import rebound.

periods.analysis: 2026-Q1 came in at 1,120,991 TEUs, down 84,979 from 2025-Q4, and it remains green by a slim 991 TEUs. This is the quarter where I want everyone’s eyes open: the result meets the target, but the cushion is thin after vessel bunching, fog delays at the sea buoy, and a short labor reallocation during cruise turnaround weekends. The winter maintenance on cranes C-12 through C-15 was necessary and kept the assets healthy, yet it also reduced flexibility during two large Asia service calls. Green is green, but this one should be treated as a near-threshold operating warning.
periods.recommendations: Protect the green position by creating a Q2 berth resiliency roster that separates cruise weekend labor coverage from container surge coverage. Finish crane C-15 commissioning checks before the next Asia string call and require daily readiness signoff during the first two weeks of April. Hold the extra-loader berth windows only for carriers that can commit to balanced import and export moves, because low-yield empty surges will not give us enough target cushion.

periods.analysis: 2026-Q2 improved to 1,154,225 TEUs, up 33,234 from 2026-Q1, restoring a healthier green margin above the 1,120,000 target. The rebound came from better berth separation, cleaner crane availability after the winter maintenance cycle, and stronger export bookings from the resin and refrigerated food shippers we have been courting since the 2025-Q1 yellow quarter. Gate 6 continued to pay dividends, and the North Intermodal Yard saw fewer missed rail cutoffs after the Tuesday-Friday block train schedule was adjusted. The arc is encouraging: we absorbed a warning quarter, corrected the operating constraints, and are again growing from a more reliable base.
periods.recommendations: Make the Q2 berth resiliency roster the standard summer model and include a written escalation path for fog, storm surge advisories, and cruise-container labor conflicts. Advance design and procurement for Gate 3 OCR expansion, using Gate 6 performance as the benchmark for truck turn-time savings. Commercial Development should now pursue two balanced-service commitments for late 2026, with contract language tying incentives to loaded export growth and schedule reliability.

periods.analysis: Container volume increased from 1,154,225 to 1,166,000 TEUs, above the 1,120,000 target. The gain is favorable, but gate and berth capacity must keep pace.
periods.recommendations: Preserve berth separation and truck appointment controls while reviewing the delayed cargo-gate automation milestones.
